## Span and linear independence {#sec-solutions-span-independence}

Exercises from @sec-span-independence.

[**1.**]{#solution-span-independence-1}

(a) The line through the origin in the direction $(1, 2)\T$.

(b) All of $\R^2$: the two vectors don't lie along the same line ($\det\mat{1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1} = -5 \neq 0$).

(c) The $xy$-plane in $\R^3$.

(d) The line through the origin in the direction $(1, 1, 1)\T$: the second vector is twice the first.

[Back to exercise 1](../part-3/14-span-independence.qmd#exercise-span-independence-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-span-independence-2} Yes. Solving $c_1(1, 1, 1)\T + c_2(1, 2, 3)\T = (3, 4, 5)\T$: the first two entries give $c_1 + c_2 = 3$ and $c_1 + 2c_2 = 4$, so $c_2 = 1$ and $c_1 = 2$, and the third entry checks: $2 + 3 = 5$. So $(3, 4, 5)\T = 2(1, 1, 1)\T + (1, 2, 3)\T$.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-3/14-span-independence.qmd#exercise-span-independence-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-span-independence-3}

(a) Dependent. Row reduction of the matrix with these columns goes
$$
\mat{1 & 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 5 & 8 \\ 3 & 6 & 9}
\xrightarrow[R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - 3R_1]{R_2 \,\leftarrow\, R_2 - 2R_1}
\mat{1 & 4 & 7 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 \\ 0 & -6 & -12}
\xrightarrow{R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - 2R_2}
\mat{1 & 4 & 7 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0},
$$
leaving no pivot in column 3. Take $c_3 = 1$: the second row gives $-3c_2 - 6 = 0$, so $c_2 = -2$, and the first gives $c_1 - 8 + 7 = 0$, so $c_1 = 1$. The relation is $(1, 2, 3)\T - 2(4, 5, 6)\T + (7, 8, 9)\T = \zerovec$.

(b) Independent: the matrix with these columns has determinant $1(4 - 1) - 0 + 1(0 - 2) = 1 \neq 0$.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-3/14-span-independence.qmd#exercise-span-independence-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-span-independence-4} Two vectors in $\R^2$ are dependent exactly when the matrix they form has determinant zero: $4 - k^2 = 0$, so $k = 2$ or $k = -2$. (For $k = 2$, $(2, 4)\T = 2(1, 2)\T$.)

[Back to exercise 4](../part-3/14-span-independence.qmd#exercise-span-independence-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-span-independence-5}

(a) Suppose $c_1\vect{v}_1 + c_2\vect{v}_2 = \zerovec$. Then $c_1\vect{v}_1 + c_2\vect{v}_2 + 0\vect{v}_3 = \zerovec$, and independence of all three forces $c_1 = c_2 = 0$.

(b) Suppose $a(\vect{u} + \vect{v}) + b(\vect{u} - \vect{v}) = \zerovec$. Rearranging, $(a + b)\vect{u} + (a - b)\vect{v} = \zerovec$, so by independence $a + b = 0$ and $a - b = 0$, which give $a = b = 0$.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-3/14-span-independence.qmd#exercise-span-independence-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-span-independence-6} $\zerovec$ satisfies $0 + 0 + 0 = 0$. If $\vect{p}$ and $\vect{q}$ have entries adding to 0, so do $\vect{p} + \vect{q}$ (the sums add) and $k\vect{p}$ (the sum is multiplied by $k$). So the plane is a subspace. The plane $x + y + z = 1$ is not: it doesn't contain $\zerovec$.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-3/14-span-independence.qmd#exercise-span-independence-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-span-independence-7}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import null_space

V = np.column_stack([[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1], [2, 3, 2]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(V))              # 3 < 4: dependent
c = null_space(V)
print(c.ravel() / c[0, 0])                   # scaled so that c1 = 1
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(V[:, :3]))       # 3: the first three are independent
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
V = [1 0 1 2;
     2 1 0 3;
     0 1 1 2];
rank(V)                    % 3 < 4: dependent
c = null(V);
c = c / c(1)               % scaled so that c1 = 1
rank(V(:, 1:3))            % 3: the first three are independent
```

```{.text .code-output}
ans =

     3

c =

    1.0000
    1.0000
    1.0000
   -1.0000

ans =

     3
```
:::

Four vectors in $\R^3$ must be dependent. The relation is $\vect{v}_1 + \vect{v}_2 + \vect{v}_3 - \vect{v}_4 = \zerovec$: the fourth vector is the sum of the other three. The first three have rank 3, so they are independent.

[Back to exercise 7](../part-3/14-span-independence.qmd#exercise-span-independence-7){.sol-link}

## Basis, dimension and change of basis {#sec-solutions-basis-change}

Exercises from @sec-basis-change.

[**1.**]{#solution-basis-change-1}

(a) Not a basis: $(2, 4)\T = 2(1, 2)\T$, so the vectors are dependent.

(b) A basis of $\R^2$: the determinant is $4 - 6 = -2 \neq 0$.

(c) Not a basis of $\R^3$: two vectors can't span a space of dimension 3. (They are a basis for the $xy$-plane.)

(d) A basis of $\R^3$: the determinant is 2 (@sec-span-independence, Example 3).

[Back to exercise 1](../part-3/15-basis-change.qmd#exercise-basis-change-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-basis-change-2} Solve $c_1 + c_2 = 4$ and $2c_1 + 3c_2 = 7$. Subtracting twice the first from the second gives $c_2 = -1$, so $c_1 = 5$: $[\vect{v}]_B = (5, -1)\T$. Check: $5(1, 2)\T - (1, 3)\T = (4, 7)\T$. ✓

[Back to exercise 2](../part-3/15-basis-change.qmd#exercise-basis-change-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-basis-change-3} The third vector is the sum of the first two, and the first two are not parallel. So $(1, -1, 0)\T$ and $(0, 1, -1)\T$ form a basis, and the dimension is 2. (The span is the plane $x + y + z = 0$, the subject of Exercise 4.)

[Back to exercise 3](../part-3/15-basis-change.qmd#exercise-basis-change-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-basis-change-4} The equation gives $x = -y - z$, with $y$ and $z$ free, so every point of the plane is $y(-1, 1, 0)\T + z(-1, 0, 1)\T$. These two vectors are independent, so they form a basis, and the dimension is 2.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-3/15-basis-change.qmd#exercise-basis-change-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-basis-change-5} Take $\vect{b}_1 = (1, 1)\T$ along the line and $\vect{b}_2 = (-1, 1)\T$ at right angles to it. The projection keeps $\vect{b}_1$ and sends $\vect{b}_2$ to $\zerovec$, so in this basis its matrix is $\M{B} = \mat{1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0}$. With $\M{P} = \mat{1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1}$ and $\M{P}^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mat{1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1}$,
$$
\M{A} = \M{P}\M{B}\M{P}^{-1} = \mat{1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\mat{1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1} = \frac{1}{2}\mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1}.
$$
Check: $\M{A}(1, 1)\T = (1, 1)\T$ and $\M{A}(-1, 1)\T = \zerovec$. ✓

[Back to exercise 5](../part-3/15-basis-change.qmd#exercise-basis-change-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-basis-change-6} $\M{B}^2 = (\M{P}^{-1}\M{A}\M{P})(\M{P}^{-1}\M{A}\M{P}) = \M{P}^{-1}\M{A}(\M{P}\M{P}^{-1})\M{A}\M{P} = \M{P}^{-1}\M{A}^2\M{P}$. Geometrically: doing the transformation twice is the same transformation whichever coordinates you describe it in, so its matrix in the new basis is the new matrix squared.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-3/15-basis-change.qmd#exercise-basis-change-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-basis-change-7}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

p = np.array([1, -1, 0]) / np.sqrt(2)
q = np.array([1, 1, -2]) / np.sqrt(6)
u = np.array([1, 1, 1]) / np.sqrt(3)
P = np.column_stack([p, q, u])

th = np.radians(120)
Rz = np.array([[np.cos(th), -np.sin(th), 0],
               [np.sin(th),  np.cos(th), 0],
               [0, 0, 1]])
print(np.round(P @ Rz @ P.T, 10) + 0)
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
p = [1; -1; 0] / sqrt(2);
q = [1; 1; -2] / sqrt(6);
u = [1; 1; 1] / sqrt(3);
P = [p q u];

Rz = [cosd(120) -sind(120) 0;
      sind(120)  cosd(120) 0;
      0 0 1];
round(P * Rz * P', 10)
```

```{.text .code-output}
ans =

     0     0     1
     1     0     0
     0     1     0
```
:::

The result is exactly $\M{C}$. In the basis $\vect{p}, \vect{q}, \vect{u}$, the rotation is the simple $\M{R}_z(120°)$; the change of basis carries it over to the usual coordinates.

[Back to exercise 7](../part-3/15-basis-change.qmd#exercise-basis-change-7){.sol-link}

## Column space, null space and rank–nullity {#sec-solutions-fundamental-subspaces}

Exercises from @sec-fundamental-subspaces.

[**1.**]{#solution-fundamental-subspaces-1} Row 2 is twice row 1, so the echelon form is $\mat{1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0}$, with rank 1. The column space has basis $(1, 2)\T$. With $x_2 = s$ and $x_3 = t$ free, $x_1 = -2s - 3t$, so the null space has basis $(-2, 1, 0)\T$ and $(-3, 0, 1)\T$. Rank–nullity: $1 + 2 = 3$, the number of columns. ✓

[Back to exercise 1](../part-3/16-fundamental-subspaces.qmd#exercise-fundamental-subspaces-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-fundamental-subspaces-2} Row 3 is row 1 plus row 2, so $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_1 - R_2$ makes it zero. Rows 1 and 2 already have their pivots in columns 1 and 2, with zeros above and below, so the reduced form is $\mat{1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0}$, with rank 2.

- Column space: $(1, 0, 1)\T$ and $(0, 1, 1)\T$, the pivot columns.
- Null space: with $x_3 = t$, $x_1 = -2t$ and $x_2 = -t$, so the basis is $(-2, -1, 1)\T$.
- Row space: $(1, 0, 2)$ and $(0, 1, 1)$.
- Left null space: row 1 plus row 2 minus row 3 is zero, so the basis is $(1, 1, -1)\T$.

The null space is at right angles to the row space: $(1, 0, 2) \cdot (-2, -1, 1) = 0$ and $(0, 1, 1) \cdot (-2, -1, 1) = 0$. ✓

[Back to exercise 2](../part-3/16-fundamental-subspaces.qmd#exercise-fundamental-subspaces-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-fundamental-subspaces-3} One equation in three unknowns: $x_1 = 6 - 2x_2 - 3x_3$, with $x_2 = s$ and $x_3 = t$ free. So
$$
\vect{x} = \mat{6 \\ 0 \\ 0} + s\mat{-2 \\ 1 \\ 0} + t\mat{-3 \\ 0 \\ 1}.
$$
The solutions form a plane in $\R^3$, parallel to the null space, which is the plane $x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 0$ through the origin.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-3/16-fundamental-subspaces.qmd#exercise-fundamental-subspaces-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-fundamental-subspaces-4} Independent columns means rank 4. So the column space has dimension 4 (inside $\R^6$), the null space dimension $4 - 4 = 0$, the row space dimension 4 (all of $\R^4$) and the left null space dimension $6 - 4 = 2$. Since the null space is $\{\zerovec\}$, $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ has at most one solution: exactly one if $\vect{b}$ is in the column space, and none otherwise.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-3/16-fundamental-subspaces.qmd#exercise-fundamental-subspaces-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-fundamental-subspaces-5} If every $\vect{b}$ in $\R^m$ can be reached, the column space is all of $\R^m$, which has dimension $m$. The dimension of the column space is the rank, so $\operatorname{rank}\M{A} = m$. The rank is also at most the number of columns, so $m \le n$.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-3/16-fundamental-subspaces.qmd#exercise-fundamental-subspaces-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-fundamental-subspaces-6} If $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$ then $\M{A}\T\M{A}\vect{x} = \M{A}\T\zerovec = \zerovec$. Conversely, if $\M{A}\T\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$, then
$$
0 = \vect{x}\T\M{A}\T\M{A}\vect{x} = (\M{A}\vect{x})\T(\M{A}\vect{x}) = \lVert\M{A}\vect{x}\rVert^2,
$$
and a vector of length zero is $\zerovec$, so $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$. So the two null spaces are the same.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-3/16-fundamental-subspaces.qmd#exercise-fundamental-subspaces-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-fundamental-subspaces-7}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import null_space, orth

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
A = rng.standard_normal((5, 3)) @ rng.standard_normal((3, 8))
m, n = A.shape
r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(A)
print("rank", r)
print("column space", orth(A).shape[1], " null space", null_space(A).shape[1],
      " row space", orth(A.T).shape[1], " left null space", null_space(A.T).shape[1])
print("largest row . null vector:", np.abs(A @ null_space(A)).max())
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
A = randn(5, 3) * randn(3, 8);
r = rank(A)
dims = [size(orth(A), 2), size(null(A), 2), size(orth(A'), 2), size(null(A'), 2)]
max(abs(A * null(A)), [], 'all')     % tiny: rows are perpendicular to the null space
```

```{.text .code-output}
r =

     3

dims =

     3     5     3     2

ans =

   8.0939e-16
```
:::

The dimensions are $r = 3$, $n - r = 5$, $r = 3$ and $m - r = 2$, as the table predicts, and every row dotted with every null space vector gives zero, up to rounding error of about $10^{-15}$.

[Back to exercise 7](../part-3/16-fundamental-subspaces.qmd#exercise-fundamental-subspaces-7){.sol-link}

## Orthogonality and least squares {#sec-solutions-orthogonality-least-squares}

Exercises from @sec-orthogonality-least-squares.

[**1.**]{#solution-orthogonality-least-squares-1}

(a) $(1, 2, 2) \cdot (2, 1, -2) = 2 + 2 - 4 = 0$, so the angle is $90°$.

(b) The dot product is 1 and both lengths are $\sqrt{2}$, so $\cos\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}$ and $\theta = 60°$.

[Back to exercise 1](../part-3/17-orthogonality-least-squares.qmd#exercise-orthogonality-least-squares-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-orthogonality-least-squares-2} $\vect{a} \cdot \vect{b} = 9$ and $\vect{a} \cdot \vect{a} = 3$, so $\vect{p} = 3\vect{a} = (3, 3, 3)\T$. The error is $\vect{e} = (-1, 0, 1)\T$, and $\vect{e} \cdot \vect{a} = -1 + 0 + 1 = 0$. ✓

[Back to exercise 2](../part-3/17-orthogonality-least-squares.qmd#exercise-orthogonality-least-squares-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-orthogonality-least-squares-3} With $\M{A} = \mat{1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2}$ and $\vect{y} = (6, 0, 0)\T$, the normal equations are
$$
\mat{3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5}\mat{c \\ m} = \mat{6 \\ 0}.
$$
Subtracting the first from the second gives $2m = -6$, so $m = -3$ and $c = 5$: the line is $y = 5 - 3t$. The errors are $6 - 5 = 1$, $0 - 2 = -2$ and $0 - (-1) = 1$, so the sum of squared errors is $1 + 4 + 1 = 6$.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-3/17-orthogonality-least-squares.qmd#exercise-orthogonality-least-squares-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-orthogonality-least-squares-4} $\M{A}\T\M{A}$ is symmetric, so its inverse is too, and
$$
\M{P}\T = (\M{A}\T)\T\big((\M{A}\T\M{A})^{-1}\big)\T\M{A}\T = \M{A}(\M{A}\T\M{A})^{-1}\M{A}\T = \M{P}.
$$
And
$$
\M{P}^2 = \M{A}(\M{A}\T\M{A})^{-1}(\M{A}\T\M{A})(\M{A}\T\M{A})^{-1}\M{A}\T = \M{A}(\M{A}\T\M{A})^{-1}\M{A}\T = \M{P}.
$$
Geometrically, $\M{P}\vect{b}$ is already in the column space, and projecting a vector that is already in the subspace leaves it where it is.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-3/17-orthogonality-least-squares.qmd#exercise-orthogonality-least-squares-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-orthogonality-least-squares-5} $\lVert\vect{a}_1\rVert = 3$, so $\vect{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{3}(1, 2, 2)\T$. Then $\vect{q}_1 \cdot \vect{a}_2 = \tfrac{1}{3}(1 + 0 + 2) = 1$, so
$$
\begin{aligned}
\vect{v}_2 &= \vect{a}_2 - \vect{q}_1 = (1, 0, 1)\T - \tfrac{1}{3}(1, 2, 2)\T \\
&= \tfrac{1}{3}(2, -2, 1)\T,
\end{aligned}
$$
which already has length 1. So $\vect{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{3}(2, -2, 1)\T$. Check: $\vect{q}_1 \cdot \vect{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{9}(2 - 4 + 2) = 0$. ✓

[Back to exercise 5](../part-3/17-orthogonality-least-squares.qmd#exercise-orthogonality-least-squares-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-orthogonality-least-squares-6} The normal equations say $\M{A}\T\vect{e} = \zerovec$, where $\vect{e} = \vect{y} - \M{A}\hat{\vect{x}}$. The first column of $\M{A}$ is all 1s, so the first row of $\M{A}\T$ is all 1s, and the first entry of $\M{A}\T\vect{e}$ is $e_1 + e_2 + \dots + e_k = 0$.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-3/17-orthogonality-least-squares.qmd#exercise-orthogonality-least-squares-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-orthogonality-least-squares-7}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

t = np.array([0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5])
h = np.array([2.1, 7.6, 11.3, 11.8, 10.5, 6.2])
A = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(t), t, t**2])
c, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, h, rcond=None)
print(np.round(c, 3))
print("g is about", round(-2 * c[2], 2), "m/s^2")
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
t = [0; 0.5; 1; 1.5; 2; 2.5];
h = [2.1; 7.6; 11.3; 11.8; 10.5; 6.2];
A = [ones(6, 1), t, t.^2];
c = A \ h
g = -2 * c(3)
```

```{.text .code-output}
c =

    2.0214
   14.0186
   -4.9286

g =

    9.8571
```
:::

The fit is $h \approx 2.02 + 14.02t - 4.93t^2$. Comparing with $h_0 + ut - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ gives $\tfrac{1}{2}g \approx 4.93$, so $g \approx 9.86$ m/s², close to the true value of about 9.81.

[Back to exercise 7](../part-3/17-orthogonality-least-squares.qmd#exercise-orthogonality-least-squares-7){.sol-link}

## Part III review {#sec-solutions-review-3}

Exercises from the [Part III review](../part-3/review.qmd).

[**1.**]{#solution-review-3-1} *Uses @sec-span-independence and @sec-determinants.* They are dependent:
$$(1, -1, -1) = (2, 1, 0) - (1, 2, 1).$$
The first two are not parallel, so all three span a plane through the origin. Its normal is $(2, 1, 0) \times (1, 2, 1) = (1, -2, 3)$, so the plane is $x - 2y + 3z = 0$. The matrix with these columns has determinant 0, because its columns are dependent: it flattens space onto this plane.

[Back to exercise 1](../part-3/review.qmd#exercise-review-3-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-review-3-2} *Uses @sec-basis-change and @sec-invariant-lines.* Solve $c_1(1, 1) + c_2(1, -1) = (5, 1)$: $c_1 + c_2 = 5$ and $c_1 - c_2 = 1$, so the coordinates are $(3, 2)$. With $\M{P} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1}$,
$$\M{P}^{-1}\M{S}\M{P} = \mat{1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1}.$$
$\M{S}$ is the reflection in $y = x$. The first basis vector lies along the mirror line, so it stays put, and the second is perpendicular to it, so it is reversed. In a basis made of invariant directions, the matrix is diagonal.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-3/review.qmd#exercise-review-3-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-review-3-3} *Uses @sec-fundamental-subspaces and @sec-gauss-jordan-rank.* $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ gives $\mat{1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1}$, and then $R_1 \leftarrow R_1 - R_2$ gives the reduced row echelon form $\mat{1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1}$. So the rank is 2, with pivots in columns 1 and 3.

- Column space: the pivot columns $(1, 2)$ and $(1, 3)$ of $\M{A}$, which span all of $\R^2$.
- Row space: $(1, 2, 0)$ and $(0, 0, 1)$, the nonzero rows of the reduced form.
- Null space: $x_2$ is free, with $x_1 = -2x_2$ and $x_3 = 0$, so the basis is $(-2, 1, 0)$.
- Left null space: only $\zerovec$, since the column space is all of $\R^2$.

Rank–nullity: $2 + 1 = 3$, the number of columns, and $2 + 0 = 2$, the number of rows. $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ is solvable for every $\vect{b}$, because the column space is all of $\R^2$, but the solution is never unique: any multiple of $(-2, 1, 0)$ can be added to it.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-3/review.qmd#exercise-review-3-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-review-3-4} *Uses @sec-orthogonality-least-squares.* With
$$
\M{X} = \mat{1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3}, \qquad \vect{y} = \mat{1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 4},
$$
the normal equations $\M{X}\T\M{X}\vect{c} = \M{X}\T\vect{y}$ are
$$\mat{4 & 6 \\ 6 & 14}\mat{c_0 \\ c_1} = \mat{12 \\ 23},$$
with solution $c_0 = 1.5$, $c_1 = 1$: the line is $y = 1.5 + x$. The fitted values are $1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5$, so the residuals are $-0.5, 0.5, 0.5, -0.5$. They add up to zero (orthogonal to the column of 1s), and $0(-0.5) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.5) + 3(-0.5) = 0$ (orthogonal to the column of $x$ values).

[Back to exercise 4](../part-3/review.qmd#exercise-review-3-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-review-3-5} *Uses @sec-orthogonality-least-squares.* With $\M{A}$ having columns $(1, 0, 1)$ and $(0, 1, 1)$,
$$\M{A}\T\M{A} = \mat{2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2}, \qquad \M{A}\T\vect{b} = \mat{1 \\ 2},$$
so $\hat{\vect{x}}$ solves $2\hat{x}_1 + \hat{x}_2 = 1$ and $\hat{x}_1 + 2\hat{x}_2 = 2$. Twice the second minus the first gives $3\hat{x}_2 = 3$, so $\hat{\vect{x}} = (0, 1)$, and the projection is $\vect{p} = \M{A}\hat{\vect{x}} = (0, 1, 1)$. The error $\vect{e} = \vect{b} - \vect{p} = (1, 1, -1)$ is orthogonal to both columns, and the distance is $\lVert\vect{e}\rVert = \sqrt{3}$. (Check: the plane's normal is $(-1, -1, 1)$, and $\lvert\vect{b} \cdot \vect{n}\rvert / \lVert\vect{n}\rVert = 3/\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{3}$.)

[Back to exercise 5](../part-3/review.qmd#exercise-review-3-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-review-3-6} *Uses @sec-basis-change, @sec-inverses and @sec-invariant-lines.* $\M{A}(1, 1) = (5, 5)$ and $\M{A}(1, -2) = (2, -4)$, so $\M{A}\M{P} = \M{P}\mat{5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2}$, and
$$\M{P}^{-1}\M{A}\M{P} = \mat{5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2}.$$
The lines through $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -2)$ are invariant lines of $\M{A}$: it stretches the first by a factor of 5 and the second by a factor of 2. In Part IV these directions are called eigenvectors.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-3/review.qmd#exercise-review-3-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-review-3-7} *Uses @sec-fundamental-subspaces and @sec-span-independence.*

a. The null space has dimension $7 - 4 = 3$, the column space and row space have dimension 4, and the left null space has dimension $5 - 4 = 1$.
b. No. The column space is a 4-dimensional subspace of $\R^5$, so some $\vect{b}$ are out of reach: exactly those with a nonzero component along the left null space.
c. Three, one for each dimension of the null space.
d. No. Seven vectors in $\R^5$ are always dependent; equivalently, the null space is not just $\zerovec$.

[Back to exercise 7](../part-3/review.qmd#exercise-review-3-7){.sol-link}

[**8.**]{#solution-review-3-8} *Uses @sec-orthogonality-least-squares.*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

def gram_schmidt(A):
    A = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)
    Q = np.zeros_like(A)
    for j in range(A.shape[1]):
        v = A[:, j] - Q[:, :j] @ (Q[:, :j].T @ A[:, j])   # remove projections
        Q[:, j] = v / np.linalg.norm(v)
    return Q

A = np.array([[1, 1, 0], [1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1]])
Q = gram_schmidt(A)
print(np.round(Q, 4))
print("Q^T Q = I:", np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(3)))

Q2, R2 = np.linalg.qr(A)
print("Same columns up to sign:", np.allclose(np.abs(Q2), np.abs(Q)))
```

## MATLAB

Save the function as `gram_schmidt.m`:

```matlab
function Q = gram_schmidt(A)
    Q = zeros(size(A));
    for j = 1:size(A, 2)
        v = A(:, j) - Q(:, 1:j-1) * (Q(:, 1:j-1)' * A(:, j));   % remove projections
        Q(:, j) = v / norm(v);
    end
end
```

Then:

```matlab
A = [1 1 0; 1 0 1; 0 1 1];
Q = gram_schmidt(A)
fprintf('Q''*Q = I: %d\n', norm(Q'*Q - eye(3)) < 1e-12)
[Q2, R2] = qr(A);
fprintf('Same columns up to sign: %d\n', norm(abs(Q2) - abs(Q)) < 1e-12)
```

```{.text .code-output}
Q =

    0.7071    0.4082   -0.5774
    0.7071   -0.4082    0.5774
         0    0.8165    0.5774

Q'*Q = I: 1
Same columns up to sign: 1
```
:::

The built-in QR may choose the opposite sign for some columns. Either sign gives an orthonormal basis for the same space.
